The cloud AI would occasionally translate a German weekly plan into English and return an entirely English training record — "old PCs dismantled" instead of the German wording. The instructions sent to the model were written in German throughout, but never said which language to answer in. Of the four writing styles, exactly one mentioned German in passing; the other three, including the default bullet points, left the question open.

The language is now stated explicitly and follows the app: the German version produces a German report, /en/ produces an English one. This applies to all four writing styles.

There is also a rule for your own notes: whatever you write in the weekly plan field is not translated and its technical terms are not swapped out. "Active Directory" stays "Active Directory". The phrasing may be adapted to the chosen writing style, the content may not be replaced.

An English weekday name in the answer no longer makes the day disappear either. Previously only the German name was recognised; anything else was silently dropped and replaced with generated text.
changelog_en.6.4.17:
The weekly plan is read instead of being overwritten

The report book assistant has a field where you simply write down your week — "Mon: removed old PCs, set up three new ones. Tue: worked through tickets. Fri: vocational school, topic subnetting". Without an internet connection, none of it reached the report. The text was matched against a list of twelve office terms — invoice, delivery note, warehouse, customer and the like — and anything not on it was silently discarded. For an IT trainee, a nurse or a car mechanic that meant the entire text was gone, without any notice, and the report filled up with generic phrasing.

Rather than extending the list, there is no list any more. What you write is what the report says, in your own words, without rewording. Day markers are now evaluated: "Mon:" goes to Monday, "Tue:" to Tuesday. Previously only the cloud AI could do this; offline, the text was spread over two random days. The generator then tops the day up as before, so every day stays complete.

If a day mentions vocational school, that day counts as a school day — even if a different day was selected above. The selection above is visibly moved along, so that two places never claim different things. A subject you name yourself ("topic subnetting and VLAN") is used instead of one drawn from the curriculum.

Words that merely look like day names no longer mislead it: "Montage der Anlage" is not a Monday, and a training course is not vocational school. The example shown in the field now uses the notation that is actually evaluated.
changelog_en.6.4.16:
Vocational school days now arrive in the report as vocational school days

If you set, say, Thursday and Friday as vocational school in the assistant, those days often came back with general company activities instead of lesson content. When inserted into the report they then passed as ordinary working days, while a single block “Vocational school” with one sentence in it appeared below the report — a field that cannot be edited in daily mode at all.

The setting now decides on its own. If the AI departs from it, the affected day is rewritten with lesson content instead of the answer being taken at face value, and a school day nobody selected no longer appears by itself. The “School day” switch on each day is set during insertion, so Thursday and Friday are marked as vocational school in the report, in the preview and in the PDF. The extra block below is gone, because the same fact would otherwise be stated in two places.

The subject now sits on the right day instead of once for the whole week. An occupation you entered yourself also gets lesson content on its school days; previously it fell back to general activities because no subject list is stored for it. A saved draft remembers the school days as well.
changelog_en.6.4.15:
The report book's writing style can now be chosen freely

The assistant used to ask “How strict is your trainer?” and quietly derived two separate things from the answer: sentence form and amount of text. Four buttons produced only three forms and three lengths, mixed crosswise — and full sentences or continuous text were not reachable at all, whatever you picked.

There are now two separate controls, and both say what they do. “Writing style” offers bullet points in IHK style, full sentences in the third person, the first person, and continuous text as one connected paragraph per day. “Length per day” independently sets how much text is produced: short, medium or detailed.

Below the styles there is an example that updates the moment you switch and uses your own occupation. You see what a Monday looks like in that style before generating, instead of having to guess from a label.

Because every chamber and every trainer wants something slightly different, there is also a field for your own rule in plain words — for instance “present tense, not past” or “exactly four lines per day”. Whatever you write there takes precedence over the selected style.

Every style also works without an internet connection. To keep those sentences grammatically correct, the app now knows the grammatical gender of every technical term in its occupations and places the German articles correctly. Vocational school days now produce as many entries as any other day, where previously there were always only two. And sentences that repeated the same word twice no longer occur.
changelog_en.6.4.14:
Advanced options in the report assistant now show only what actually works

“Advanced options” held four controls that did nothing, or something other than they promised. The “Maximum variation” checkbox offered as a choice what is always sensible anyway — not repeating wording from earlier weeks. That now applies always, without a checkbox.

The “Writing style” block and the “Complexity” dropdown set the same value as “How strict is your trainer?” and overrode it. Switching from “Relaxed” to “Very strict” still produced the same number and depth of entries. Strictness is now the only control for this and its effect is visible: relaxed gives three to four entries per day, normal four to five, very strict six to eight.

The “Cloud AI on” switch was never read when generating — even switched off, the request went to the cloud and counted against the daily limit. Switched off, the local engine now really does the writing, with no limit and nothing leaving the device.

Also fixed: “Regenerate locally” for a single day ignored the selected training year and always wrote for the second year. An input field for your own API key and an expired beta-phase notice are gone as well; both had been invisible for a while. The calendar week now has its own section, with a note that it also decides which week the tracked hours are pulled from.
changelog_en.6.4.13:
The survey and the cloud-AI notice now appear only after the first report

Opening the report book for the first time brought up two things at once: a full-screen notice about the change of cloud AI, whose button stayed locked for five seconds, and below it the question of what a stronger AI would be worth. Both are aimed at people who already use the app — the notice explains a change there is nothing to compare without a before, and the question about value assumes you know the benefit.

Both now appear only once there is at least one report or one recorded working day. Anyone arriving for the first time goes straight to the application. Nothing changes for existing users of MyWorkLog, and anyone who has already answered or declined the survey still does not see it. Creating the first report brings up the survey right away rather than on the next visit.
changelog_en.6.4.12:
The weekly overview in the report book now shows which week is which

The strip below the key figures was 52 identical unlabelled tiles — there was no way to tell which week a tile stood for, and clicking one opened a report for a week you could not see beforehand. The overview is now grouped by month, every tile names its calendar week and date on hover, the current week is marked, and the strip can be stepped through with the arrow keys.

Three calculation errors sat in the same place: 2026 has 53 calendar weeks but only 52 were ever drawn, so the last week of the year was missing. Reports from other calendar years lit up in the current one. And drafts had the same colour as an empty week, although the legend below named a separate one for them. Clicking a tile also cleared the search field and the filters.

In the report-book assistant, a day marked as sick leave, holiday or public holiday wrote the text "undefined" into the day field — and from there into the finished IHK form. In the table of contents of the yearly PDF, "complete" and "signed" used the same character; both states are now spelled out.

The assistant had no border on any of its input fields, pickers and cards, because a colour the design referred to in eighteen places was missing. The keyboard shortcuts N, E and T opened a second dialog on top of the open one. The marker in the switch between weekly and daily format sat offset over the inactive tab.

Visible changes: the button to the shadow report book was a dark grey symbol on a dark background and practically invisible. Around a third of all buttons, fields and dropdowns rendered in the system font instead of the page font. The occupation picker, the weekdays and several messages used emoji; they now use the same icons as the rest of the app. Six close buttons had no name for screen readers.

On the English pages, 24 labels stayed German — among them the buttons for saving, printing, exporting and generating.
changelog_en.6.4.11:
The three profile fields in settings now respond across the whole row

For training occupation and federal state, a large part of the area could be clicked without anything happening. The row looked usable across its full width, but the list only opened when you hit the narrow strip holding the value itself — about a fifth of the area. Sitting exactly in the middle of the row was the explanatory hint, not the control. The whole row now responds.

The section has been rebuilt along the way. Three separately framed tiles have become one connected list; the label sits on the left and the selected value on the right, where there used to be nothing but empty space. All three rows are the same height — the name row used to be shorter than the other two because it had no hint. An entry that has not been chosen now reads quietly as “Not selected” instead of appearing in the same weight as a real value.

In the light appearance the three boxes were previously filled dark, because their background was written in directly instead of coming from the colour scheme. That is fixed.

A smaller correction on the side: on an empty profile the name field showed the word “undefined”, and closing settings saved it as the name.
changelog_en.6.4.10:
The figures on the About page are now measured, not asserted

Under the heading “Trust in numbers” there used to be four values, none of which came from a measurement: 200 users, 8,900 hours tracked and 86 % satisfaction were fixed numbers in the page source. They never changed, and they looked exactly like real ones.

They now come from the same web analytics that feed the analytics page, over a 90-day window. If that data cannot be reached, the last measured value is shown — with the date it was taken beside it.

Two cards changed along the way. Hours tracked is gone: the app stores everything in the browser on the device, so there is nobody who could count hours. In its place is the average time on site, which really is recorded. And “satisfaction” has become “engagement” — what is measured is how many visits click onward and how far, not whether anyone was satisfied. Nobody was ever asked that, so there is no score for it any more. The calculation behind it is spelled out in the card’s info panel.

The two info panels were also broken: on hover something opened up of which only the title line was visible, the rest sat behind an invisible edge. They now show their full contents.
changelog_en.6.4.9:
The FI Academy has been removed — the skill tree takes over

There were two learning areas side by side promising the same thing. Since the last update the skill tree asks real questions and only awards points for correct answers; the FI Academy sat next to it as an area nobody was developing further. Two routes to the same place is one too many, so only the better one remains.

Anyone still holding a link or bookmark to the old address now lands on the skill tree instead of an error page. The entry in quick search (Ctrl+K), the links at the end of the deep dives and the card in the IT Hub all point there as well.

The IT Hub is tidier for it: one entry card instead of two, and three figures instead of four. The streak at the top now counts days spent on the skill tree — it used to show the FI Academy streak, which had nothing to do with the skill tree.

A note for anyone who used the FI Academy: the progress recorded there still sits in the browser and is not deleted. It simply can no longer be opened, because the view for it no longer exists.
changelog_en.6.4.8:
The code report now shows the daily pattern as bars instead of a tile grid

On /repo-report/, the distribution of commits across the day used to be a tile grid: twelve columns, two rows, amount encoded as brightness. That display failed at three things. The hour axis below it did not match the tiles, because the same column meant a different time in the upper row than in the lower one. An hour without a single commit looked like an hour with one. And on hover the tile grew over its neighbours, while a second browser hint appeared on top of the tooltip.

A bar chart with 24 bars on a shared baseline now stands in its place. The hour marks sit in the same grid as the bars and can no longer drift. An empty hour is visible as a grey line. Nothing moves on hover: the column highlights itself, and the tooltip appears in its own strip above the chart, where it covers no bar.

The report also counts exactly the files that are part of the project now. Previously the header counted everything on disk while the score below counted only versioned files — two different totals on one page. The weekday and time-of-day figures now state their period, a contributor with few commits is no longer listed as 0 %, and the page no longer scrolls sideways on narrow screens.
changelog_en.6.4.7:
The skill tree now asks questions instead of accepting XP

Until now you could type your own experience points into /skill-tree/: pick a topic, enter a number, done. A level therefore said nothing about what anyone actually knew. That button is gone.

In its place is a practice round. Ten questions per session, drawn from 150 questions across 30 topics — networking, Linux and system administration, backend, DevOps, frontend and soft skills, from the OSI model through file permissions and subnetting to why an average response time misleads you. Every answer comes with an explanation, including the correct one: it says not only what is right, but why the other three options are wrong.

Whatever you answer correctly returns at growing intervals — after one day, then three, then a week and onwards, up to half a year. A wrong answer resets the interval and the question reappears within the same round. The progress card shows a preview of the next fourteen days, so what is due for retention is visible, not just what has been collected.

Every topic has three tiers. Advanced opens once the basics are solid, pro after that — not after a waiting period and not after a set number of attempts.

The training-log analysis stays and still credits topics, but with less weight: a single technical term used to be worth more points than the hardest question in the whole tree. Documented practice now counts alongside answered questions rather than above them.

The page also carries readable content for search engines for the first time: a description for each of the 30 topics, six sample questions verbatim with their solutions, an explanation of the learning system and frequently asked questions. All of it is available in English as well. Progress stays in the browser and is not transmitted anywhere.
changelog_en.6.4.6:
The code report's score measured size, not quality — it now counts real findings.

At /repo-report/ it said “Codebase health score 94/100” in large type. On inspection, 82 of those 94 points came from four figures: 25 for the project having more than 50,000 lines, 20 for the number of languages in use, 15 for having over 100 files, and 12 for being 247 days old. Dependencies even counted the wrong way round: more than 20 packages scored higher than none at all. What was being measured was how big and how old the project is — what was written above it was how healthy it is.

The score is now made of nine checks, each reporting a counted defect, and each stating its denominator right next to it: whether every JavaScript file parses, whether every reference to a file actually finds one, how much source sits in files over 1000 lines, open notes in the code, files with identical content, tests present, comment density, project paperwork, and the dependency count — this time the right way round. Size, age and language count deliberately no longer feed into it.

A new “what costs points” section names the files responsible. Currently 86 out of 100; almost all of the deduction comes from roughly half the source living in very large files.

The page is also generated during deployment now instead of being produced and copied by hand, so it is current with every update.
changelog_en.6.4.5:
The code report at /repo-report/ was flagging an error that wasn't one.

The page scans the source for open notes — markers such as TODO, FIXME or BUG in comments. Exactly one was reported, and it was a German word: one line carried the comment “inkl. 1900-Schaltjahr-Bug”, explaining how Excel counts dates. But the search did not compare whole words, only letter sequences anywhere in the line — by that rule every “debug” in the code would have counted as an open bug as well.

A false alarm in a list like that costs more than it looks: it sends the next reader into code that is fine.

While looking into it, the opposite fault turned up, and it is the worse one: lines that START with the comment — the usual way these markers are written — were counted as comments one step earlier and never searched at all. A “TODO” on its own line would never have shown up, and the page would still have reported “clean codebase”. Both are fixed and verified both ways: real markers are found, German words are not.
changelog_en.6.4.4:
The language switch is now in the dashboard quick-action bar as well.

Until yesterday the English version was reachable only through the profile menu, and since yesterday also through the footer of every page. Both assume you go looking for it: one behind a click on the profile picture, the other at the very bottom of the page. On the dashboard — the screen you see most often — the only thing visible without any action was the notice strip in the sidebar, and that one can be dismissed for good.

So the bar above the charts now carries a “Deutsch” entry, right next to “Settings”. On the German version it reads “English” and leads the other way.

It sits BEFORE “Settings” rather than after it on purpose: at phone width the bar is narrower than its contents and scrolls sideways, so the last entry ends up off screen. There are several routes to the settings — sidebar, profile menu, keyboard shortcut — and considerably fewer to the language switch.
changelog_en.6.4.3:
The English version is finally findable — and the profile menu has been rebuilt.

The app has been fully available in English for a while, under its own addresses with /en/. Search engines knew about it, people barely did: the “About us” page had twenty links and not one of them led to the English version. Unless you happened to open the profile menu in the app, there was no way to find out it existed.

So the language switch now sits in the footer — on every page, in both directions. It goes to the matching page rather than the home page: from “Import your data” it takes you straight to the English version of that same page. On the few pages with no English counterpart it does not appear at all, instead of leading into an error page.

The profile menu in the sidebar has been rebuilt. Language used to be an underlined link at the very bottom that read like a footnote; it is now a “Deutsch | English” switch directly below the appearance setting — two controls built the same way instead of a control plus a link. The line under your name now says what this profile actually is: one on this device. It used to say “Online”, which looked like a sign-in that does not exist here.

Smaller fixes in the same place: the dot on the picture in the menu was always green, even offline — the network state was only shown on the strip below it. The keyboard shortcut next to “Settings” was so faint it was useless as a hint. And the menu was slightly transparent, so you could read the content behind it.
changelog_en.6.4.2:
“Latest Updates” has been rebuilt — one line per version, with dates and search.

It used to show eight entries in full, one under the other: 880 characters per version on average, the longest 3080, some 7000 characters of continuous prose in one go. No dates, no search, no structure — if you wanted to know when a change landed, or whether there was anything at all on a given topic, there was no way to find out.

Each of the 174 versions now takes exactly one line: date, number, title. The full text expands on click, set in paragraphs. The list is grouped by month and the month headers stay pinned while you scroll.

New above the list is a release calendar: one square per calendar day, a week per column, colour by the number of releases that day. Clicking a day crops the list to it. Next to it are three counted figures — 174 versions, 52 days with a release, 14 in a single day. Search matches keywords and version numbers and highlights the hits.

That needed release dates, which did not exist before: only the date of the current version was stored. For 170 of the 174 versions the day they first appeared is recorded in the project history and was taken from there once. The remaining four have no record and sit under “No date” at the end of the list — nothing is estimated. For the same reason the calendar encodes no “release size”: the version number rolls over mechanically and says nothing about how large a release was.

The area also works in the light theme now — its colours used to be hard-wired to dark. And the five most recent entries are available in English.
changelog_en.6.4.1:
The architecture overview at /archflow/ was empty on the live site — instead of the map it showed "archflow-data.js could not be loaded". The file holding the project data sat at an address the server was only meant to reach through a rewrite rule; that rule never took effect and the request ran into a 404. The data now lives at an address that is served directly, with no rule involved — the map builds again on the German and the English page alike.

While we were there, the page got lighter: the request used to append a timestamp to the address and so pulled 248 KB fresh on every visit, even though the file rarely changes. Now the browser just asks whether there is anything new.
changelog_en.6.4.0:
The notifications area has been rebuilt. It is called "Notifications" now and reads as a log: entries are grouped by day — Today, Yesterday, and before that with weekday and date — each one with a time. Unread notifications are marked by a filled dot and a stronger title; read ones step back. That also finally makes it visible that notifications disappear on their own after seven days — they always did, it just was not written anywhere.

The settings used to take up the top half of the area: to read a notification you had to scroll past seven checkboxes first. They now sit behind the gear icon in the top right. The main switch stays visible in both views, because that is what you reach for when the notifications are bothering you.

Opening the panel no longer marks everything as read before it is drawn — that is why the highlight on new items was never visible.

The filter bar is gone. It only knew "Warnings" and "Successes" while the app produces four kinds of notification — notices and errors fell through both filters and were invisible once one was active. With a seven-day retention and a handful of entries it did not earn its place anyway.

The whole area works in the light theme now. It was the last one that stayed completely black, because its colours were hard-wired; the same was true of the short-lived toasts at the top of the screen, which were a black box with grey text in light mode. Both were also slightly transparent — you could read the dashboard through the notification.

Smaller fixes: the cross that removes a notification did not work — the id arrived as text and was compared against a number. The confirmation before "Delete all" is the app's own dialog instead of the system window. The badge on the bell no longer pulses non-stop. And notification text is escaped before it is put into the page.
changelog_en.6.3.19:
The daily notice "Your last backup is more than 7 days old" was wrong for everyone who backs their data up to the cloud. The timestamp of the last backup was not written where the upload happens, but in three button handlers next to it. Auto-sync calls the upload function directly and none of those buttons — so it had been uploading successfully for years without that being recorded anywhere. The reminder therefore appeared every day while the data was in fact being saved every few minutes. The record is now written inside the upload function itself, so every route to the cloud counts as a backup, including the automatic one. "Last backup" also states where the data went — cloud or file.

The wording was wrong too: it asked for a file export even though a cloud backup is just as good. It now reads either "There is no backup of your data yet — neither in the cloud nor as a file" or "Your last backup is more than 7 days old".

Second, the notifications can actually be switched off now. The alerts area had five checkboxes, exactly one of which was ever read. The afternoon check, the end-of-day reminder, the Friday notice, the weekly plan and the two milestone messages appeared regardless of any setting and could not be turned off anywhere. There is now a main switch, "Notifications", that silences everything at once — including the prompt to back up to the cloud. When it is off, the individual checkboxes below are visibly disabled instead of merely dimmed. Two missing individual switches were added, for the daily reminders and for the milestones. Feedback on your own actions ("Saved", "Copied") is unaffected.

Also fixed: the long-shift warning had never fired. It compared an entry's date ("2026-08-28") against a differently formatted current date ("28.8.2026") — a comparison that could never match. The checkboxes in the alerts area now use the accent colour you picked instead of a hard-wired blue-violet, and the icon on the backup notice is an icon rather than the word "save".
changelog_en.6.3.18:
The IHK view has been rebuilt. It used to be a cockpit of five numbers — progress, two countdowns, target hours for the entire apprenticeship and two grades — with a form underneath. None of them answered the question you actually bring to this page: will I be admitted to the final exam, and what is still missing?

That is what stands at the top now: the three admission requirements for the final examination under the German Vocational Training Act, checked one by one. Training time completed, intermediate exam taken, training record kept, entry in the register of apprenticeship contracts. Each item states where it comes from — from the law, from a chamber guideline, or from your own entries. The app cannot know about the register entry; it is shown as "not measurable" and waits for you to confirm it, rather than being green on the assumption that it is fine.

Below that, the apprenticeship runs as a time band across its whole length, split into training years, with the real milestones: start, end of the probation period, intermediate exam, registration deadline, final exam, end of contract — each with its date and its distance from today.

Three calculation errors were fixed along the way. The absence rate divided by calendar days instead of training days; on a five-day week that produced a figure about a third too low, and a percentage that is too low looks exactly like a correct one. The denominator is now stated next to it: this many sick days out of this many training days, with public holidays and leave taken out. School days were listed under "absences" — but vocational school is training time, not absence, so it now sits in the time breakdown. And the grade bar filled to (6 minus grade) divided by 5, which made a five look like almost full progress; a grade is a position on a scale and is now shown as one, with the mark at 4.0.

End of contract and exam date are two separate fields now. The final-exam field was locked and simply took over the end date — but at most chambers the exam falls months earlier, so the countdown was showing the wrong day. Added as well: the probation period with its end date, a field for the chamber's registration deadline, a list of weeks with no entry plus a route into the training record, the split of training time across company, vocational school, leave, illness and public holidays, and the average grade from the school view.

Two things that did not work at all before: in the light theme this was the only page that stayed completely black — it brought its own darkness along and had not a single rule for light mode. And it loaded two extra fonts just for itself; it now uses the app's own, with the monospace face reserved for measured values instead of the whole text.
changelog_en.6.3.17:
The history view has been rebuilt. There used to be a filter box above the list with two empty date fields — you had to know which period you wanted to see before you could see it. Now there is a time band: one column per week across your entire record, height equal to hours worked, the faint trace behind it the target for the same week. You can see at a glance when things were busy and where the gaps are — and you simply drag out the range you want to read, with the mouse or a finger. Clicking a month band in the list crops to that month as well. The exact dates are below and can still be typed in when you need to hit a specific day.

The type filters now show how many entries sit behind them, and they follow what actually occurs in the chosen period. More importantly: custom entry types are finally included. The filter bar was a fixed list of the seven built-in types — if you created your own type, you could never filter for it.

Search understands operators: ">8" finds every day over eight hours, "<6" everything below, "#CustomerPortal" searches the project field, and both combine with plain search text. Whatever was recognised is spelled out in a line below the field — otherwise an operator would be indistinguishable from a search word with no hits. The / key jumps into the search field. The old "Min. h" field is gone in exchange. Also new: a sort order (date, longest days, largest surplus, largest deficit), a job filter when you have several jobs, and a switch for row height.

The list itself is now a table with labelled columns instead of a row of cards: the same screen holds well over twice as many entries, numbers line up under each other, and between hours and balance there is a small deviation bar — a full swing equals one whole day's target. Month and day stay pinned at the top with their totals while you scroll, as does the filter bar. Very long histories are loaded in blocks instead of being built all at once.

Two bugs fixed along the way: the notes column used to show the complete stored text, including the part the app generates itself ("07:30-16:30 (8.00h)") — so the time span appeared twice in the row, once as text and once as a number of hours. The column now shows only your own note; if you did not write one, it shows the shift times. And every row had a coloured border all the way round: a narrow stripe on the left edge was intended, but the colour was set on all four sides. With mixed entries the list looked like a stack of coloured stickers.

The detail view of an entry now also shows the time span, break, target hours and the job, and appears as a card on wide screens instead of a bar at the bottom of the window.
changelog_en.6.3.16:
The commuting-costs page now lets you set the route yourself. Until now it always used the shortest connection the routing service suggests - if you drive a different way, because the bypass is quicker or the town centre is jammed in the morning, there was no way to record that.

Now you simply drag the line on the map onto your own route. A point appears where you drop it, and you can move it again or remove it with a click; on a phone, tapping the line sets the point. The calculation still follows real ways: the points steer the route, and the kilometres still come from the way network rather than a straight line. Distance, travel time, fuel costs, the CO2 comparison and the commuter allowance all follow your route, and the Google Maps link carries the waypoints along.

An important bug fixed along the way: choosing "Bike" did not actually calculate a bike route. The previous routing service only knows roads for cars and quietly returned the same car route for bike and on foot - cycle paths never appeared in it, and a point you tried to place on a cycle path snapped to the nearest road. It was hard to notice, because a car route looks plausible on a bike too. Now each mode has its own routing service (the same ones OpenStreetMap itself uses): car, bike via cycle paths, and walking via footpaths. On the Stuttgart-Ludwigsburg route that is 15.8 km in 22 minutes by car and 18.8 km in 59 minutes by bike - previously the same number appeared twice. This also means bike and walking now show a real time; under "On foot" the field is labelled walking time. There is still no line routing for buses and trains - that is now stated as a note instead of passing the road distance off as a timetable.

Below the map you also see how your route compares with the shortest connection. That matters, because the German commuter allowance is based on the shortest road route (§ 9 (1) sentence 3 no. 4 Income Tax Act) - a longer one only counts if it is clearly quicker in practice and you use it regularly. Both figures are shown side by side, rather than letting the yearly total come out too high without saying so.

Smaller fixes: the hint on the map now describes the action available at that moment, and it is no longer hidden on narrow screens - there is no hover there, so it would otherwise be the missing piece. Start and destination markers have their own screen-reader labels again; the map library had replaced them with a generic "Map marker".
changelog_en.6.3.15:
Six icons in the sidebar were broken or meaningless. Graphify showed a double-headed arrow instead of a graph, the IT Hub an unfinished shape from a foreign icon set, and the guide a clock face without hands. Untis, travel costs and the privacy policy are new as well - the policy's shield was the exact same drawing as the rights checker one row above it, two entries with one picture. All six also apply to the command search (Ctrl+K) and to "Start app tour" in the profile menu.

An outdated icon has been removed from the app manifest: a purple-and-teal clock from an earlier version of the brand that no longer resembles the current mark. It was the only entry without a fixed size, so installing the app could have picked it over the correct artwork. The Apple home screen icon now points at the correct artwork too.
changelog_en.6.3.14:
The imprint and the privacy policy can now be reached from every public page. Nine pages had no route there at all - the report book, the FI Academy, the skill tree, the rights checker and the architecture view had no footer whatsoever. This is not cosmetic: an imprint has to be reachable from every page.

On six pages the shared footer showed "v…" instead of the version number, because the script that loads it was missing. The English pages also carried "Daten uebernehmen" in German, and the date beside it was formatted the German way ("26. August 2026" instead of "26 August 2026"). Both now follow the language of the page.

On the analytics page, the green dot next to "Live activity" always claimed the list was current - even when the request had failed. The ticker then froze silently while still looking like it was running. If the request fails it now reads "Unavailable" and the dot stops pulsing. The map controls there also had no visible keyboard focus at all.

The Christmas page has been removed. Nothing on the site linked to it and it was excluded from search, so it was effectively unreachable - a dress-up toy with nothing to do with time tracking. Anyone still holding a link to it now lands on the home page.
changelog_en.6.3.13:
Two addresses on this site only worked if you capitalised them exactly right. /Impressum/ served the page, /impressum/ an error - the same for /DSGVO/ and /Fachinformatiker/. Web addresses distinguish upper and lower case, and the imprint and the privacy policy are precisely the two addresses people type out rather than click. Typed, they are almost always lower case. Both spellings now lead to the page.

The Christmas page never snowed. It requested three files that are not at the given path - the snowflake instructions were among them. A browser does not report that visibly; the page builds itself, just without whatever the missing file would have brought. A fourth file was loaded although the page uses nothing from it. The paths are corrected, the needless request is gone, and it snows again.

On the same page four button labels were cut off: "Handschuhe" became "Handschu", "Augenbrauen" became "Augenbra". The words were wider than their tile and were silently clipped at the edge - on a dress-up toy that means you can no longer see which part you are clicking. Long words are now hyphenated instead of clipped, and the labels are set a touch smaller so the shorter ones stay in one piece.

In the English version four passages were still in German - in the rights checker, the report book, the shadow report book and the switching page. The rights checker was the most conspicuous case: the caution note under the results was a German sentence whose bold terms were already English.
changelog_en.6.3.12:
Every close and dismiss button now shows a real icon instead of the text character ×.

That sounds like a detail, but it was visible. The × is a mathematical symbol, and typefaces do not set it centred: inside a 32-pixel button it sat two and a half pixels too low, and at six pixels tall it was noticeably smaller than it looked like it should be. The button was not at fault - no amount of centring would have helped, because the browser aligns the text box, not the character inside it.

39 buttons were affected across the app, the report book and the shadow report book: closing dialogs, dismissing notices, removing holiday ranges, goals and jobs. They now sit exactly centred and share the same size and stroke weight as the rest of the icons.

Also in the contract manager: the net salary calculator had two dropdowns, tax class and federal state, that had no effect on the result. The code never read them - the figure beside them stayed the same whatever you picked. Both are gone.

Instead of a single number, the calculator now shows what it actually computes: social contributions as an amount, and beside it income tax left open as "not calculated". The rough tax formula that used to be built in has been removed, because income tax depends on your tax class and cannot be estimated honestly without it. The result is therefore labelled "Net before income tax" - on training salaries that is usually the net figure already. Amounts now also carry thousands separators, as they do everywhere else on the page.
changelog_en.6.3.11:
The 404 error page now has a look of its own. The purple accent is gone; the page is greyscale on black throughout, and white appears only where there is something to do - the button back into the app, and the logo. The reason is simple: anyone who lands here has mistyped something or followed an old link. At that moment the page should be quiet and point the way back, rather than looking like a regular part of the app.

Second, the page now speaks English as soon as the address you called starts with /en/. Until now, English-speaking visitors got a fully German error message after a typo.

The bottom left also shows the address that was actually requested, which helps if you want to pass on or report a broken link. The green status dot that used to sit beside it is gone: it claimed all systems were operational without ever checking.
changelog_en.6.3.10:
The "About" page has been rebuilt as a landing page that tells its story as you scroll.

At its centre is a section called "A day with MyWorkLog": a day card stays pinned on the left while four steps move past on the right - clock in, break, clock out, report book. As you scroll, the card's bar fills, the break is carved out of it, and the week's balance appears together with a finished report-book entry. It is the same day shown at the top of the page: 07:30 to 16:30, a 30-minute break, 8:30 hours worked, half an hour of flextime.

Before this, almost nothing moved. Three separate reveal mechanisms sat on top of each other and overwrote one another, leaving a brief fade. Now exactly one place writes to each element, and the reveals run staggered on a proper easing curve. The headline rises out of a mask line by line, the tickers pick up speed when you scroll faster, and on wide screens a rail down the left edge reads your scroll position as a time of day.

The content was tidied up as well. Sixteen cards across three grids used to repeat the same points; now each point appears once, in a grid of differently sized panels. Two claims were removed because nothing backed them up: "99.9% uptime" and "24/7 support". In their place are things that are true - that the app runs without a connection, and that it stays free.

Smaller additions: a skip link, visible keyboard focus rings, an active marker in the navigation, and if you have reduced motion enabled in your system, you now get gentle fades without any movement. The English version is fully translated, including the tickers, which used to stay German.
changelog_en.6.3.8:
The commuting-costs page has been rebuilt from scratch, in the same language as the year view: hairlines instead of cards, large figures, one picture per section.

The number that actually matters now sits at the top - the commuter allowance over a year - with distance, travel time, trips and fuel cost beside it. The three assumptions behind it (working days, fuel price, consumption) are an editable sentence directly underneath rather than a form further down: if you can see the number, you can see that you may change it.

The commute-distance ring is gone. It filled against a fixed ceiling of 80 kilometres that came from nowhere, so a half-full ring meant nothing. In its place the statutory tiers are drawn as a bar: 30 cents up to kilometre 20, then 38, with the threshold marked and both amounts on the segments.

The CO2 comparison is sorted by amount and the values sit beside the bars instead of inside them - for the bike, zero used to be invisible. Also: every emoji replaced by an icon, the page now runs in the app's typeface, start and destination markers are symbols rather than pictographs, and the shared footer is finally there.

Three fixes: a travel time is only shown for the car, because the open routing service carries the car profile alone and returns the same car route for bike and on foot - the page now says so. The list of connections existed twice in the code and was overwritten by the older version on the first routing request. And the route now stays on the map when switching between light and dark.

The English version has been brought along, including the text that is only created in the browser; numbers and month names there follow the page language.
changelog_en.6.2.22:
The intro film froze on a single frame — on the server, not locally. The reason: scrubbing sets the playback position about thirty times a second. Each set is a jump to a different point in the file, and while only the beginning was loaded, every jump needed its own network request. Before one finished the next arrived and cancelled it — none ever completed. On your own machine this never shows, because there every request is answered instantly.

The film is now loaded once in full and scrubbed from memory afterwards, so every jump is immediate regardless of the connection. Scrubbing also waits for the previous jump to finish.
changelog_en.6.2.21:
The intro film sat still. It was fully loaded and error-free — but the part that makes it follow your scrolling was never armed. It hangs off an event the browser fires once the video data is ready; if the file is already in the cache, that event has come and gone before the script starts listening.

It only became visible now because the first frame of the new film faded in from black over half a second — frozen there, you saw a black panel. Before, it simply froze on the same first frame, which nobody noticed.

Fixed at both ends: readiness is now queried directly rather than only waited for, and the film starts without a fade — a video that follows your scrolling has no beginning; every point is a scroll position.
changelog_en.6.2.20:
Video now bypasses the service worker. Until now it fetched every file with a forced network request, to guarantee a fresh copy after an update. That is right for a few kilobytes of JavaScript and CSS; for the 2.4 MB intro film it meant a full re-download on every page load — plus, while scrolling, many small partial requests that all went around the cache.

The browser can buffer and reuse parts of a video on its own. It is allowed to do that again. The version number in the address is what guarantees the new film arrives after an update.
changelog_en.6.2.19:
After a deploy, devices that had already visited kept showing the old intro film — even after a cache purge at Cloudflare. The cause: the file was served as “one year, immutable”. That rule is meant for the icons in the same folder, which never change under the same name; the video does exactly that. “Immutable” means the browser does not even ask — and a purge clears Cloudflare, not the device.

The video address now carries the version number, like every other file. After each update it is a new address that no device can have cached. The video is also no longer served as immutable.
changelog_en.6.2.18:
The button at the end of the intro is new: instead of the filled pill it is now a wordmark with an underline that grows in from the left on hover, and an arrow that slides right along with it. Pressing it gives a short give.

On devices without a pointer, the line and arrow sit permanently in their end position — otherwise there would be nothing on a phone to suggest the wordmark is a button at all.

Fixed along the way: the button sat flush against the text above it. The spacing was set, but the intro's base reset overrode it. That applied to the previous button too.
changelog_en.6.2.17:
The intro film is the one from 6.2.13 again. The changes from 6.2.16 have been rolled back: the stronger dimming was too dark, and the camera move pushed in too close.

The timing fix from 6.2.15 stays — each of the eight text sections sits entirely on one calm scene, with no crossfade at either end, and the film catches up faster while you scroll.
changelog_en.6.2.16:
The intro film now shows you where to look. The spotlight was so faint that at the frame's display size it no longer read as a pointing gesture — three scenes in a row therefore looked like the same dashboard. The history, performance and holiday-planner scenes had no spotlight at all.

Each scene now carries a strong spotlight on the component in question, with an accent-coloured frame around it. The screen around it stays visible — you can still tell it is an app, just dimmed.

The camera also moves toward the element instead of away from it. It used to zoom out, which brought the sidebar into view at the edge; on the history screen that looked as if it were opening. The move now travels toward each scene's target point, and on the entry list the sidebar is out of frame entirely.
changelog_en.6.2.15:
The intro film is the one from 6.2.13 again — the close-ups introduced in 6.2.14 have been rolled back. They sat too tight on the component, left almost no movement, and broke the context instead of creating it.

What stays is the fix this was actually about: the text sections came up too early. “Every entry stays findable” started at second 10.99 of the film, where the breakdown scene was still running — a dashboard shot. “Your trend, not just your today” started in the middle of a crossfade. Each of the eight sections now sits entirely on one calm scene, with no crossfade at either end.

The film also catches up faster while you scroll. The easing used to close a gap by 18 % per frame, about 0.4 seconds to catch up — scroll briskly and you were still looking at the previous scene while the new text was already there. Close to the target the motion stays smooth; further away it catches up; very far away it jumps.
changelog_en.6.2.14:
The scenes in the intro film now show what the text beside them talks about. Previously the first three scenes were the same dashboard shot with nothing but a different spotlight — at the reduced frame size the difference was invisible, and “Your trend, not just your today” simply showed the whole dashboard.

Each scene is now a close-up of the part in question: the key-figure row, the balance chart with its peak and direction, the breakdown bar with all five categories, the entry list with filters and search, the holiday pacing rings, the bridge-day suggestions.

The camera move also goes in rather than out. It used to zoom out, which brought the sidebar into view at the edge — it looked as if something were opening instead of the view closing in on the subject.

The eight text sections now sit exactly in the calm windows between the crossfades. No text is on screen during a fade, and the frame holds its position instead of briefly jumping to the wrong one.
changelog_en.6.2.13:
The intro on the start page has been rebuilt. The film used to sit behind the text as wallpaper: stretched over the full height and therefore cropped at the sides, with a 70 % scrim on top. Almost nothing of it was visible.

It now sits in its own 16:9 frame at the centre of the screen — nothing is cropped any more and the scrim is gone. The frame travels with you: large and centred at the start, then over to the left with the text beside it, and back to the centre at the end. On narrow screens the film sits on top and the text below it.

The eight text sections are timed to the six scenes in the film, so what you are looking at is what you are reading about. The captions have left the film for that reason — burnt-in text cannot be translated and showed up in German on the English page.

Gone are the mock code editor, the fake spreadsheet window and the terminal output. They competed with the product instead of showing it.
changelog_en.6.2.12:
The intro on the start page now shows the app itself instead of a generic clip. The background film that scrubs along as you scroll is built from six real captures: the dashboard with its key figures, the balance trend, the working-time breakdown, the history, the performance analysis and the holiday planner. Each scene puts a spotlight on the part being described, with a short caption.

The film has grown from 5 to 22.9 seconds and now holds 458 frames instead of 150 — scrolling is noticeably smoother because each scroll step has a frame of its own. The file still comes in at 1.8 MB, near the previous 1.7 MB.

The captures show sample data only — no real working hours, no name, no employer.
changelog_en.6.2.11:
Six icons in the “Your data is safe” dialog were drawn incorrectly. The clearest case was “Secure data transfer”: its outer arc ran past the top edge of the drawing area and was cut off there. The bin next to “Delete” and the icon above “Your control” were missing parts of their outline, “No content to third parties” showed half of a refresh arrow and sat visibly off to the right, the middle arc of the Wi-Fi icon was a straight line, and the cookie was the only icon made of filled shapes rather than strokes — at small sizes it read as a face.

All six have been replaced with the originals from the Lucide set. They now sit fully inside their drawing area and are centred, measured against the geometry that is actually rendered.

One layout bug in the same dialog went with it: the icon in the open-source note was allowed to shrink, so on narrow screens it was squeezed — at a window width of 320 pixels it came out 4.8 pixels wide instead of 16, at unchanged height. It now keeps its size, as does the round badge in the confirm button.
changelog_en.6.2.7:
The segments of the working-time split have a gap between them again. Now that the bar is sorted by share, two similar colours can end up side by side — work and school are both blue — and without a separator they read as a single segment. The gap was in the stylesheet all along but was overridden by a default of 0. Anyone who set the spacing themselves in the chart settings keeps their value.

Two things follow from it. The segments are now sized so that fills and gaps together match the width of the card exactly — otherwise the last and, since the sorting, smallest category would have lost eight pixels without anyone noticing. And the corners of the segments follow the gap rather than the rounding of the whole bar; the old value would have turned a four-percent segment into a pill.
changelog_en.6.2.6:
The logo in the top left of the sidebar leads back to the dashboard again. It used to be plain text; it is now a real button and can be reached from the keyboard.

The streak counted entries dated in the future. Anyone booking vacation in advance was shown a running streak and a personal best that had never happened on any past day. Only days up to today are counted now.

In the working-time split, the bar and the legend now share one order: largest share first. The bar used to follow a fixed category order while the legend followed the actual share, so row one and segment one meant different things. Equal shares keep their place instead of jumping on every refresh, and colour still belongs to the category, not to the position.

Also: the gear icon was drawn incorrectly and has been redrawn. The chart settings buttons now show a visible ring when focused with the keyboard.
changelog_en.6.2.0: The dashboard has been rebuilt. The four tiles at the top used to be four different constructions — two rings, a scale, a list — and none of them showed what its number was actually measured against. They now share one layout: label, value, bar, and the reference underneath. The progress rings for week and month are gone. They were misleading: the ring sat half full at zero deviation, and a full ring meant twenty hours of overtime — a warning rather than an achievement. The scale was never stated. In their place a bar now grows out of a visible zero line, to the right for a surplus and to the left for a deficit, with both ends labelled. The scale comes from your own weekly target, not from a hard-coded forty-hour week. New on the right: remaining leave as a figure of its own — previously it showed only used out of total and you had to subtract yourself. The working-time split showed the same number three times; the headline figure now gives the total, the bar the proportions, the list the individual values. With no data it used to read "0.0 Public holiday" — that is fixed too. The figures above the trend chart are down from six to three: "Current" repeated the flextime value from the top, while volatility and daily average supported no decision. The timer used to sit as a narrow column beside the form, almost empty. It belongs inside it, because that is the form it fills — it is now a bar within it, with proper icons instead of keyboard characters. And where nothing has been recorded yet, the page no longer just says "No data": it says what will appear there and how to get started. Along the way, something turned up that explains how the whole app looked: for years MyWorkLog referenced two typefaces it never loaded. The stylesheet asked for "Inter" and "JetBrains Mono", while the font that actually loaded, "Plus Jakarta Sans", was used nowhere. The app therefore ran in the operating system default, and every figure (balances, timer, tables) was set in Consolas. That is where the pocket-calculator look of values like "+22.34 h" came from. Now the app loads what it uses: Plus Jakarta Sans for text and headline figures, JetBrains Mono for the timer and measured values. Cards also stand off the background properly; previously they sat three percent lighter on it and on a laptop screen you could not see where a card began. And the working-time split now formats numbers for the page language.
changelog_en.5.9.10: The rights checker looks calmer. The page used to run on its own purple plus ten category colours that drew more attention than the answers did. It now follows the accent colour from your settings, and colour is reserved for the verdict: whether something is allowed, depends, or is not allowed. That used to be three red dots with nothing explaining what they meant - the result is now spelled out on the card. Categories carry icons instead of emoji so they look the same on every device.
changelog_en.5.9.9: Third deep dive in the IT Hub: how memory forgets. Every bit sits on a tiny capacitor that drains all by itself — the access timings, the error correction and a whole class of attack all follow from that weakness. Five diagrams do the arithmetic: the temperature slider shows why twice the refresh rate is mandatory above 85 degrees, and what happens to the bit without any refresh. A second one shows that a cell being read amounts to only a few dozen millivolts. A third replays access patterns and makes it visible why the same amount of data takes three times as long when read at random. The fourth is a real Hamming code you can click: one bit error gets repaired, two get detected, three lead to silent miscorrection. And the fifth hammers memory rows until the neighbours flip — including the protection mechanism you walk straight past if you attack enough rows at once.
changelog_en.5.9.8: Second deep dive in the IT Hub: how an SSD remembers. From the single flash cell through NAND pages and blocks to the address translation in the controller — and finally a head-to-head with the hard disk. Five diagrams compute real physics instead of decoration: the electron count follows from the threshold shift, write amplification from the fill level, the raw bit error rate from the overlap of the voltage windows. In the comparison, both drives get the same read request and work through it in slow motion: the arm seeks the track, the platter turns to the sector, while the SSD finishes over a hundred accesses alongside. Switch to a megabyte in one piece and the gap shrinks to less than threefold.
changelog_en.5.9.3: When Google reported “Error 403: access_denied” while connecting to Drive, the app showed nothing but the bare error code. It now says what that means: the Google project is still in testing mode, where only listed test users get in — not even the developer. Along with the way out, and a note that no Google review is needed for it.
changelog_en.5.9.2: The Google Drive setup was still missing the second hurdle: new Google projects start in “Testing” mode, where only listed test users get in — the project owner included. Google reports this as “Error 403: access_denied”, which sounds like a failed review. The dialog now describes both routes (add your account as a test user, or switch to “In production”) and notes that publishing needs no Google review here: the app only requests access to files it creates itself, and that permission counts as non-sensitive.
changelog_en.5.9.1: The Google Drive setup listed “https://myworklog.de” as the authorised JavaScript origin, even when the page was actually running under a different address. Copying that value got you “Error 400: origin_mismatch” from Google, with no hint as to why. The dialog now shows the address the page is really open under, with a button to copy it, plus a note that the value belongs in the “Authorised JavaScript origins” field without a trailing slash, not among the redirect URIs.
changelog_en.5.9.0: The shadow report book now keeps a verifiable record. Every entry you create, change or delete carries the fingerprint of the one before it — if something is altered, removed or slipped in later, the chain stops matching from that point on, and “Check chain” in the vault menu says exactly that. One thing to be clear about: this is not a certification. Anyone with your vault password can recompute the chain, and your device clock is freely adjustable. The proof only carries weight once you get the chain head out of the house early — email it to your works council, photograph it, show it to someone you trust; there is a copy button for that. From that moment on, what your record looked like back then is settled. Two fixes to the file preview as well: PDFs stayed a blank grey box on phones, because Android and iOS have no built-in viewer for embedded PDFs and the intended fallback text therefore never appeared — there is now a card with “Open in new tab”, where the device’s own PDF viewer takes over. And files without an extension, which is what forwarding from a phone often produces, were dismissed as undisplayable across the board; now the content decides: if there is text inside, text is shown.
changelog_en.5.8.0: The shadow report book can now back itself up to your Google Drive in one click — entries, custom categories and all evidence. What gets uploaded is the same encrypted block that “Export backup” produces: Google stores a file that is unreadable without your vault password, and the app only ever gets access to files it creates itself. Large vaults upload in parts, with real progress in megabytes instead of a guessed bar; earlier backups are listed in the dialog and can be restored or deleted from there. The file preview also covers far more than before: text files, notes and logs, CSV and Excel sheets as real tables, JSON indented, emails with sender, date and subject, plus Word, PowerPoint and OpenDocument files as a text extract. Every derived view states at the top what it was taken from and what it is missing — with evidence, the original file counts, not the extract. Formats no browser can display (HEIC, legacy .doc files) now say so by name instead of only reporting “no preview”.
changelog_en.5.7.0: The privacy policy described the “Full” feedback mode too narrowly: it mentioned device data only, while your name, usage statistics and app settings are sent as well. Section 4 now lists every single field and states plainly that this data is not anonymous, because your name is part of it — along with what is never transmitted in either mode: individual time entries, notes, project names and the shadow report book. References to “section 4” are now clickable. The data preview the policy promised did not actually exist; it does now: below the feedback box, “Which data is sent?” opens a table of every field with your real values. The consent line next to the feedback checkbox also linked to the legal notice instead of the privacy policy, and five section headings of the English version were still in German.
changelog_en.5.6.0: The trainer approval added in 5.5.0 showed an empty week: the activities were missing entirely because the page looked for the days under the wrong names. That is fixed — and so it cannot happen again unnoticed, the view now iterates over the days actually present in the link instead of a fixed list. The header also said “year 1” where the training year was meant. New: you can have several weeks approved at once, up to the entire logbook. In the approval window you pick the weeks (one click selects all open ones) and see how long the link becomes. Your trainer then decides week by week — approve or send back, with a reason — and returns a single response that applies every decision at once. The QR code still only works for a single week; beyond that it gets too dense to scan, which is what the link is for. The signature covers every individual decision, not just the name.
changelog_en.5.5.0: Your trainer can now approve a weekly training record directly — no account, no app, and nothing uploaded anywhere. You show them a QR code or send them a link; they see the week read-only on the new page myworklog.de/ausbilder and tap Approve or Send back. Their answer comes back as a short code that you scan with your phone camera. An approval locks the entry and sets it to “signed”; a return shows you right on the card what needs changing. The entire week travels inside the link itself — the part after the hash mark never leaves the device, there is no server in between and no connection that could fail on a company network. Every approval is signed on your trainer's device, so the app can tell whether a later approval came from the same device; responses altered after the fact are rejected. The lock lives in your own data — you can release it at any time, but that discards the approval. The page is available in English too.
changelog_en.5.4.0: The categories in the shadow logbook were too coarse — a lot of things only roughly fit. Instead of ten general ones there are now around forty, sorted by training content, working time and pay, conduct, safety and health, vocational school, and organisation. New entries include break not granted, rest period too short, youth employment protection ignored, pay incorrect, time off for vocational school refused, sexual harassment, threats, workplace accidents and disadvantages after a complaint. Because a list that long is useless to scroll through, you now pick a category through a search box: just type, accents do not have to match, and under each name there is a short note on when it applies. If nothing fits, you can create your own category straight from the search — it is then available on every later entry, can be renamed, and is stored encrypted in the vault, so it travels with backups and cloud sharing. A category still used by entries cannot be deleted; the app tells you how many use it. Important for the record: the notes under the names are purely a selection aid and do not appear in the PDF or TXT export — only the category name does. Also reworked: the time-basis block in the entry form was the heaviest part of the dialog, with two large explanation cards. It is now a plain two-row choice, and the explanation below it refers only to the axis you have currently selected.
changelog_en.5.3.1: In the shadow logbook's exported record, the severity overview ran as a thin bar in the header of every page — and from page two onwards it sat on top of the text. The reason: a repeated header does not push the body text down, it overlays it. Nothing of this was visible on screen; the fault only appeared in print. The header is now gone. The confidentiality marking, the case reference and the severity overview each appear exactly once, on the cover page — where they already were, the header merely repeated them. Page numbers still come from the print dialog via “Headers and footers”.
changelog_en.5.3.0: The date and time on a shadow logbook entry were ambiguous. The form prefilled the date field with the current moment when you created an entry, yet everything downstream treated that value as the time of the incident — so the card ended up showing a number that could mean two different things depending on the entry. Every entry now carries both timestamps, visible and labelled: the time it was recorded, set automatically and not editable, and the time it happened, which you enter yourself. Which of the two leads the chronology — the card heading, the sort order, the period filter and the export — is up to you, via the „Timeline“ switch in the toolbar. This matters most when the entries go to the chamber of commerce: the recording time shows the record was kept promptly, while the incident time is the fact the case is actually about. Individual entries may depart from the default; the choice sits in the entry form, and entries dated differently are marked in the list and in the record. The incident date is also no longer mandatory: if you are no longer sure of the day, leave it empty instead of guessing — the entry then runs on its recording time and you can fill the date in later. The exported record states its time basis at the top and prints both timestamps with every incident, so a reader never has to guess what a date means.
changelog_en.5.2.1: The shadow logbook's PDF export now carries the evidence with it. Until now only photos made it into the record; a chat log or mail export appeared with nothing but its file name and size, so the content — the actual evidence — was missing. Text-based attachments (TXT, CSV, log, EML, JSON) are now reproduced verbatim; very long files are visibly truncated rather than silently cut. Images get a caption so it is clear what a photo belongs to. New is an index of exhibits at the end of the document: every item of evidence carries a continuous exhibit number referenced from the body text, and the table states per exhibit whether it is reproduced in the record or supplied separately. PDF, audio, video and office files cannot technically be rendered into a print page — they are now clearly listed as "supplied separately" with a number instead of disappearing into a subordinate clause, and the document explains that you hand them over in original form via "Export backup". Also closed: a file name containing quotation marks could break out of the image caption in the generated export document and inject foreign markup there. Since that document holds the decrypted evidence, hardening it matters. Besides the export this also affected the display of attachments and custom fields inside the vault.
changelog_en.5.2.0: New: the vacation planner. It answers where a few vacation days buy you the longest unbroken break, calculated from the public holidays of your federal state and your own weekly schedule rather than a generic list. Every suggestion names the window, the holidays behind it, the cost in vacation days and the return (days off per vacation day spent); one click on "Book" enters exactly the days needed, leaving weekends and public holidays untouched since those cost you nothing anyway. Suggestions never overlap and fit into your remaining budget together. The planner deliberately only proposes real bridge days: taking any random week off always yields nine days off for five vacation days, which is not an insight and therefore stays out of the list. A holiday falling on a weekend does not justify a suggestion either, because it saves no vacation day. There is also a year calendar showing public holidays, booked leave and the suggestions — suggestions as an outline, booked days as a fill, so the two stay distinguishable with colour vision deficiency and in black and white print. Find it in the sidebar under "Vacation planner" and via the vacation tile on the dashboard. Also fixed: the Easter calculation was wrong. This affected Good Friday, Easter Monday, Ascension Day, Whit Monday and Corpus Christi — in 2027 Easter was three weeks off, in 2025 and 2028 a week each. It also affected automatic holiday booking. The calculation is now verified against twenty years. If you already booked holidays for an affected year, please check them once.
changelog_en.5.0.2: Cloud sharing in the shadow report book now states clearly what it does not do. It transfers the entries only — photos, PDFs, letters and recordings stay on the device where they were stored. On a second device you will see the entry, but not the file that belongs to it. Until now this was just one of four equally weighted bullet points and got lost between three reassuring statements. It now sits as its own highlighted notice directly above the password field, together with the one way to bring the files along after all: export a backup here and import it on the other device via “Import backup”. The button for that sits right next to it. While sharing is switched on, the notice also appears in the vault menu below the toggle — where you can find it again later without reopening the dialog.
changelog_en.5.0.1: The shadow vault did not arrive on a second device even though cloud sharing was on. Two bugs were behind it. The first affected the very first download on a new device: when writing data back, each item is checked for whether it has been shared — but the sharing setting itself arrives in the same pass. If the vault came before it in the order, the setting was not yet present at the moment of the check and the vault was discarded silently. Whether it hit you depended on whether you had turned sharing on before or after creating the vault. Sharing settings are now written first, then everything that depends on them. The second bug came with the storage move in version 5.0.0: the vault has since lived in the browser's database, while cloud sync still keeps its copy alongside it. A freshly downloaded state was therefore overlooked whenever the device already held a vault — and on the next save the older state even overwrote the newer one in the cloud. Both are fixed. When two states meet they are now merged rather than replaced: entries that exist on only one side are both kept, and if the same entry was edited on both devices the newer version wins — the older one moves into that entry's change history and is not lost. Evidence files still do not travel; if they are missing on this device the vault now says so explicitly instead of showing an empty preview. If the cloud holds a vault with a different password, nothing is touched. Also corrected: the privacy policy still listed IndexedDB as “currently not used”, although evidence has been stored there since 5.0.0.
changelog_en.5.0.0: The shadow report book has no storage limit any more — and it now accepts any file, not just photos. Until now it reported “out of storage space” after roughly eight images and refused to take anything else. The cause was how it was built: the whole vault sat in a single browser entry, and images were stored inside it as text — a conversion that inflates every file by a third, applied twice over. A 300 KB photo ended up taking 530 KB, and the space available was just under 5 MB. The vault now lives in the browser's database and stores files as what they are. Instead of 5 MB you get the free space on your disk, usually several gigabytes. There are no fixed ceilings left: none on the size of a single file, none on how many go into one entry. How you divide that space between photos, letters and recordings is up to you — the vault menu only shows how much is used and how much is left. Also new is what you can store: PDFs, scanned warnings, contracts, payslips, printed emails, voice messages. PDFs can be viewed right inside the vault. Every file is stored unchanged, and photos are no longer shrunk after the fact — a re-encoded image loses its capture data and is easier to challenge as evidence. You add files through a drop area now, either by choosing them or by dragging them in. Two further changes: changing the vault password now takes a fraction of a second regardless of how much you have stored, because it no longer re-encrypts every file. And backups now include the evidence — previously a backup would have saved only the text while looking complete. Existing vaults are migrated automatically the next time you unlock; the old copy is deleted only after the new one has been proven readable. Cloud sharing still carries the entries only, evidence stays on the device — to move it to a second device, use a backup.
changelog_en.4.9.0: The shadow report book can now travel with the cloud — and the “forgot password” button does something again. The button first: it did open the reset dialog, but the dialog sat invisibly behind the lock screen. From the outside it looked like nothing happened. Fixed. New is cloud sharing in the vault menu: confirm once with your vault password and the vault rides along with the app's normal cloud sync from then on, up and down. Note something down at work, carry on writing at home. Only the encrypted block is uploaded: the key is derived from your password and never leaves your device, what sits on the server is random numbers. One important point, and this used to be different: until this version the vault was uploaded with every cloud sync without being asked, because the sync simply collects the entire browser storage. Encrypted, yes, but without anyone having agreed to it. From now on it stays on the device unless you explicitly share it — and when you turn sharing off, the copy disappears from the cloud with the next upload. The privacy policy now covers the vault as its own point: what is encrypted, that it stays on the device unless shared, and what happens when sharing is turned off.
changelog_en.4.8.10: In the support area the changelog can now be expanded in full. Previously it showed the last eight versions and the rest was simply unreachable — that is 93 of 101 entries. A button below the list reveals them all; since 101 entries would stretch the page enormously, the expanded list gets its own scroll area instead of pushing everything below it out of reach. The list also became calmer in colour. Entries used to cycle through six colours based on their position in the list, so the colour meant nothing and shifted as soon as you expanded. Two of those tones were already taken: red means error and delete throughout the app, green means done, and blue and amber are the colours of vocational school and public holiday. Every fifth version therefore looked like a problem. All entries are neutral now, and colour marks exactly one thing: which version you are currently running. Also fixed: the changelog texts of the last four versions were missing all German umlauts. That was a mistake when writing the entries, not in the display — the texts are now set correctly.
changelog_en.4.8.9: The privacy policy now looks like a document rather than an advertisement. The text itself is unchanged — only its presentation: calm surfaces instead of coloured gradients in the background, an ordinary heading instead of gradient type, a full-width header bar instead of a floating pill, and the table of contents as a tidy list instead of colourful pills.
